terminal.description: A shell in your workspace where the demo runs each search on a small array.

tasks.title: Lower and upper bound
tasks.description:
Implement `lowerBound(items, target, compare?)` and `upperBound(items, target, compare?)` in `src/bounds.ts`. `items` is sorted by `compare` and may hold duplicates. `compare` defaults to `natural` from `src/compare.ts`.

- `lowerBound` is the first index `i` with `compare(items[i], target) >= 0`.
- `upperBound` is the first index `i` with `compare(items[i], target) > 0`.
- When no index qualifies, both return `items.length`. An empty array gives `0`.

The check covers duplicates, missing values, both ends, empty arrays and a custom `compare`. It also counts calls to `compare` on an array of a million objects: each search may use at most 42.
nextSteps: Keep a range `low` to `high` that always contains the answer.
Halve it on each step by comparing the middle item with target.
Write `upperBound` by changing a single comparison.
Run `node src/demo.ts` and read the first line.
hints: Let `high` start at `items.length`, not `items.length - 1`, since `items.length` is a valid answer.
If the middle item already qualifies, the answer is the middle or to its left. If not, it is strictly to the right.
Loop while `low < high`; on a qualifying middle set `high = mid`, otherwise `low = mid + 1`. When the loop ends, `low` is the answer.

tasks.title: Count and insert position
tasks.description:
Implement `countOccurrences(items, target, compare?)` and `insertPosition(items, target, compare?)` in `src/count.ts`.

- `countOccurrences` is how many items compare equal to `target`.
- `insertPosition` is where `target` can be inserted so `items` stays sorted, after any items equal to it.

You may import from `./bounds.ts`. The check counts `compare` calls on a million items where half of them equal the target: each call may use at most 84, so stepping through the duplicates is too slow.
nextSteps: Work out what the two bounds of a value tell you about its run.
Write both functions using the bounds from task 1.
Run the demo and read the second line.
hints: Both answers come from the searches you already wrote, without any extra loop.
The run of equal items starts at one bound and ends just before the other.
The count is `upperBound - lowerBound`. Inserting after equal items means inserting where the first larger item is.

tasks.title: Search a rotated array
tasks.description:
Implement `searchRotated(items, target, compare?)` in `src/rotated.ts`. `items` held distinct values in sorted order and was then rotated: a prefix moved to the end, for example `[1, 3, 5, 7, 9]` became `[7, 9, 1, 3, 5]`. The rotation may be 0.

- Return the index of `target`, or `-1` when it is not there.
- `compare` may be called with any two values.

The check covers no rotation, values on both sides of the rotation point, two items, one item, an empty array and a custom `compare`. On a million rotated objects each search may call `compare` at most 126 times.
nextSteps: Draw a rotated array and mark where the middle can land.
Show that one half around the middle is always sorted.
Decide whether the target can be in that sorted half, and keep the right half.
Run the demo and read the third line.
hints: Compare the first item of the range with the middle item. That tells you which half is in order.
In a sorted half, checking whether target lies inside it takes two comparisons with its ends.
If the left half `low..mid` is sorted and target is between `items[low]` and `items[mid]`, search left, otherwise right. Mirror that when the right half is the sorted one.
